steps.title: Heat damage
steps.body: A wine stored too warm, or left in a hot car, can taste cooked: stewed, jammy fruit, flat and dull. The cork may push out or wine may leak around it. The damage is permanent. Even a few hours above 30 degrees can harm a delicate wine.

steps.title: Light strike and refermentation
steps.body: Light strike happens when light, especially ultraviolet, reacts with riboflavin and amino acids in wine, creating sulphur compounds that smell of cabbage or wet wool. Clear glass offers no protection; Champagne in clear bottles is especially at risk. Refermentation, when yeast restarts in a bottle with sugar, gives unwanted fizz and cloudiness.

steps.prompt: Why are clear glass bottles risky for wine?
options: They let in light that can cause light strike
steps.explanation: Clear glass doesn't filter ultraviolet light, which can create cabbage-like sulphur compounds.

steps.title: Not faults
steps.body: Some things look alarming but are harmless: tartrate crystals, called wine diamonds; sediment in old reds or vintage Port; a slight haze in unfiltered wines; small bubbles in young whites bottled with some carbon dioxide on purpose. Learning these prevents rejecting good bottles.

steps.prompt: Which are harmless rather than faults?
steps.explanation: Light strike and heat damage are real faults.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Heat damage gives cooked fruit and pushed corks
Light strike gives cabbage smells; refermentation gives fizz
Crystals, sediment and slight haze are harmless
